what_it_does: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a class of AI models that reason over graph-structured data — nodes connected by edges — and are used in materials science to predict properties of atoms and molecules without running expensive physics simulations. While large language models (LLMs) have grown to billions of parameters and dramatically improved through scale, GNNs for materials modeling have stayed small (millions of parameters), and no one has systematically studied how they improve as they get larger. This paper builds a billion-parameter GNN trained on terabyte-scale datasets and borrows training techniques developed for LLMs (efficient batching, data and model management at scale) to make that training feasible. It explores three separate dimensions of scaling — model size (more parameters), dataset size (more training data), and training methodology — to establish empirical 'scaling laws' that tell researchers what accuracy to expect as each dimension grows. Based on the abstract, this lays groundwork for treating materials-modeling GNNs with the same scale-first philosophy that transformed language AI.
